claims.text: The initial high-entropy nanoalloy has a random distribution of multiple elements in a single phase at room temperature.
High-temperature annealing activates diffusion processes in the nanoalloy.
An oxygen-free inert atmosphere avoids oxidation artifacts during high-temperature exposure.
High configurational entropy creates an intrinsically disordered lattice.
The configurationally disordered lattice undergoes uniform lattice distortion with an associated defect structure.
Uniform lattice distortion reduces effective atomic diffusion coefficients.
Reduced atomic diffusion prevents phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
Reduced atomic diffusion prevents elemental segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Preventing phase separation and elemental segregation maintains chemical homogeneity and overall structure.
Compared with a lower-configurational-entropy control, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit reduced elemental segregation after identical annealing.
Compared with the control, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit minimal phase separation after identical annealing.
The annealed high-entropy nanoalloy will preserve its lattice parameters and a homogeneous microstructure.
The predicted stabilization applies up to approximately 0.8 times the melting temperature when oxidation is minimized.
Interactions among specific alloying elements could modulate high-temperature stability.
Failure to reduce segregation or maintain greater microstructural homogeneity than the lower-entropy control, despite observed lattice distortion, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
